blocks.text: You can hear a teacher talking in the next classroom through an open door, but you cannot see him. Both sound and light left the same room through the same doorway — yet only one of them bent round the frame to reach you. The reason is the enormous difference in their wavelengths.

blocks.markdown:
All waves — water, sound, light — obey the same four behaviours. Learn them once and they apply everywhere.

**Reflection:** the wave bounces back off a barrier. The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and speed, frequency and wavelength are all unchanged. Only the direction changes.

**Refraction:** the wave changes speed on entering a new medium, and therefore bends. Because the frequency is fixed by the source, the wavelength changes in proportion to the speed.

blocks.title: Diffraction
blocks.text: The spreading out of a wave as it passes through a narrow gap or round the edge of an obstacle. Diffraction is most pronounced when the width of the gap is comparable to the wavelength of the wave. Frequency, wavelength and speed do not change during diffraction — only the shape of the wavefront does.

blocks.markdown:
### Why sound bends round corners but light does not

A typical speech sound has a wavelength of about $1\ \text{m}$ — roughly the width of a doorway. The gap and the wavelength are comparable, so the sound spreads widely on the far side.

Visible light has a wavelength of about $5 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}$, which is around two million times smaller than a doorway. The gap is enormous compared with the wavelength, so the light passes almost straight through and casts a sharp shadow.

blocks.title: Interference
blocks.text: When two waves of the same frequency overlap, their displacements add. Where they arrive in phase the resultant amplitude is large — constructive interference. Where they arrive exactly out of phase the displacements cancel — destructive interference. The sources must be coherent, meaning they have the same frequency and a constant phase relationship.

blocks.title: Predicting interference from a path difference
blocks.prompt: Two coherent loudspeakers emit sound of wavelength 0.50 m. At a certain point, the path from one speaker is 1.50 m longer than the path from the other. Decide whether the sound there is loud or quiet.

steps.text: Write down the path difference and the wavelength.
Express the path difference as a number of wavelengths.
Compare with the two conditions. Three is a whole number, so the path difference is exactly 3λ.
This matches the constructive condition, so the waves arrive in phase and reinforce each other.
State the conclusion. Had the path difference been 1.75 m, that is 3.5λ, the point would have been quiet.

blocks.answer: Loud — constructive interference, since the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths

blocks.markdown:
### Standing (stationary) waves

When two identical waves travel in opposite directions along the same line — typically an incident wave and its own reflection — they interfere to produce a **standing wave**. Its pattern does not travel.

- **Nodes** are points of permanently zero displacement, where the two waves always cancel.
- **Antinodes** are points of maximum displacement, where they always reinforce.

The distance between two adjacent nodes (or two adjacent antinodes) is exactly $\frac{\lambda}{2}$. This is the fact you use to get a wavelength out of a standing-wave measurement.

blocks.title: WAEC and JAMB tip
blocks.text: Interference and diffraction happen only with waves, so observing them is the standard proof that something is a wave. If a question asks which phenomenon shows that light is a wave, the answer is interference or diffraction, never reflection — particles reflect too.

points: Reflection changes only direction; speed, frequency and wavelength are unchanged.
Refraction changes speed and wavelength but never frequency, which is why the wave bends.
Diffraction is the spreading of a wave at a gap or obstacle, and is greatest when the gap is comparable to the wavelength.
Constructive interference needs a path difference of nλ; destructive needs (n + ½)λ, and the sources must be coherent.
In a standing wave, adjacent nodes are half a wavelength apart.
